profiles.limits: One system, prompt and domain are studied. Retrieval and generation variability are conflated, and web drift cannot be excluded. training.branching: Controlled branching from a shared saved agent or retrieval state is not established. Permutations reorder existing reports for analysis rather than create new interactive trajectories.

profiles.name: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts

openness: Agents choose probe inputs and whether to probe before sequential evaluation batches.
Procedural generation spans four scenario domains and four specified rule families.
The paper provides 256 evaluation episodes and states that 1,000 training episodes are provided.
Code release under MIT and dataset distribution under a Creative Commons license are announced.
profiles.focus: Proactive hidden-rule discovery and adaptation to unannounced rule drift. Deterministic synthetic rules generate action utilities; scenario labels do not represent real experiments or new physical measurements.
profiles.limits: Agents know the candidate rule families. Drift is restricted to within-family factor replacement and direction reversal. Each episode has 12 batches of 8 cases. Page 16 allows at most one probe call per window with at most 16 cases, while pages 14–15 give inconsistent additional budget descriptions. Live physical interaction and executed research experimentation are absent.

training.reward: Probe Batch returns utilities for all four actions on agent-designed cases; Submit Action Batch returns utility feedback for selected actions. A fixed utility function rewards action anchors close to the hidden intervention score. Evaluation uses exact optimal-action accuracy, utility-based calibrated accuracy, and factor/change recognition against known rules. A training set is provided, but a policy-training algorithm or optimization run is not established.
training.reset: Episodes begin with task descriptions, field ranges, action choices, and rule-family definitions. Agent-requested episode reset, rewind, or state restoration is not established.
training.branching: Dataset construction creates a shared pre-drift prefix followed by IID and targeted post-drift branches. Agent-controlled runtime branching or cloning is not established; runtime presents a fixed sequence of batches.

profiles.name: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments

openness: Systems choose preprocessing, analysis methods, models, tools, and workflow structure within a specified scientific objective and dataset scope.
Queries provide staged Parquet files and named numerical metrics. Files are shared across queries within a task; query scopes vary.
Source citations are withheld from evaluated systems. Cached single-agent reference values are used by the training evaluator.
profiles.focus: Executed scientific data analysis and modeling on fixed recorded Earth science datasets, including training and comparing predictive models. The benchmark contains 100 tasks and 2,067 scoped queries, with 492 held out for testing. Eleven general-control tasks use synthetic or general tabular data. These are computational research tasks; the environment does not collect new physical measurements or simulate a physical laboratory.
profiles.limits: The evaluator grades reported numerical metrics. Its finite-value, positive-number, and sentinel checks do not independently establish correct code execution or computation. Test queries reuse the same underlying tasks and files, establishing scope generalization rather than unseen-task transfer. Reported inference costs omit workflow-training costs, and token accounting is incomplete.

training.reward: Pages 7 and 17 define a continuous evaluator-side reward averaged over query metrics: 0.10 numeric sanity + 0.40 inequality-target satisfaction + 0.50 cached-reference agreement, clipped to [0, 1] and adjusted for metric polarity. A zero candidate value against a nonzero reference receives zero reward. Missing references cause the remaining terms to be renormalized; page 17 reports weights of 0.40 and 0.60. Per-task and per-category optimization use training and validation query pools. At test time, pages 6 and 15–16 score each task as realistic-output rate times mean metric pass rate among realistic outputs, then sum across tasks. Realistic outputs require parsable finite metrics, at least one positive value, and no −1 sentinel.
training.reset: Not established: the supplied body does not specify workspace cleanup, random-state reset, or restoration between attempts. Repeated candidate evaluation on fixed staged datasets is described.
training.branching: Candidate-workflow search is supported, including AFlow's Monte Carlo tree search over operator graphs on page 7. Environment snapshotting, cloning, rollback, and branching from an intermediate execution state are not established.

profiles.name: ST-Bench: A Spatial-Temporal Benchmark for Multi-Agent System Generation on Scientific Research Tasks

openness: Agents freely explore designated training games; training is restricted to the first installment of each series.
Training supplies no task exemplars, demonstrations, documentation, or game-specific extrinsic rewards; intrinsic task- and game-agnostic reward shaping is permitted.
Execution tests reveal natural-language tasks at specified gameplay states; Playthrough evaluates continual learning in two fan-made games.
The paper states that the emulation package, save states, and screen captures are released; ROMs are excluded.
profiles.focus: Self-improvement through interaction with deterministic emulated video games: 500 execution tasks across ten games and end-to-end playthrough in two fan-made games. Button actions produce rendered screen observations. Feedback comes from executed emulator rules, without new physical measurements.
profiles.limits: Completion checks require distinctive visible screens, biasing tasks toward immediate visual feedback. Evaluation termination signals success and supplies no failure termination signal. Prior game knowledge can contaminate results; knowledge checks do not establish complete absence of contamination. The games evaluate embodied gameplay rather than executed scientific research experiments.

training.reward: No extrinsic game-specific training reward is provided. Intrinsic task- and game-agnostic shaping is allowed. The curiosity baseline rewards screen novelty using one minus the maximum cosine similarity to buffered frame embeddings. Skill discovery uses the agent's own success judgments to retain practice trajectories for behavioral cloning. Evaluation uses task-specific binary completion functions based on screen-reference matching, task completion gain, and playthrough progress markers; these completion functions are distinct from training rewards.
training.reset: Page 14 establishes exact reset: every episode loads a complete emulator save-state snapshot, and resetting restores it exactly. The same save state and action sequence reproduce the same trajectory. Skill practice returns to a task's starting state and applies random buttons before another attempt. Curiosity buffers reset each episode to their generation-specific initial contents.
training.branching: Exact save-state reset supports reproducible alternative action sequences from the same starting snapshot. The world-model baseline compares predicted next observations for all possible actions. A dedicated emulator cloning or arbitrary mid-trajectory fork interface is not established in the supplied pages.

profiles.name: GameBoyWorlds: A Testbed for Self-Improvement in Embodied Video Games

openness: Free-text answers over a fixed corpus and question set.
The paper claims code and data availability on page 1; availability was not independently checked.
profiles.focus: Evidence reasoning, cross-source and temporal conflict resolution, and recognition of insufficient evidence. The environment comprises 7,140 simulated workplace records across 30 projects grounded in public papers and reports, with 1,613 questions. Historical versions are stored records, not a live evolving workplace (pages 2–6).
profiles.limits: The evaluated interaction retrieves a fixed top-k context and supplies it to the answering model, ordered by timestamp and ID; it does not establish autonomous investigation or workspace modification (pages 6 and 24). Feedback comes from synthetic records and reference answers, with automatic judging. Source documents may describe experiments, but this benchmark does not execute them or obtain new physical measurements. Simulated enterprise records are not an interactive scientific simulator. LLM generation, validation, and judging can leave errors; human validation includes 50 accepted questions (pages 5 and 10).

training.reward: A training reward or online learning loop is not established. Evaluation uses GPT-5.6 Luna to compare the question, reference answer, and model response, accepting semantically equivalent answers and correct abstentions; overall and task-level accuracy are reported (pages 6 and 24).
training.reset: Environment reset support is not established. Evaluation uses a fixed retrieval corpus with retained historical record versions; those versions do not establish reset functionality.
training.branching: Agent-controlled branching or state forking is not established. Historical revisions and alternative retrieval budgets are evaluation data and settings.

profiles.name: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records

openness: Fixed multiple-choice questions with predicted audio and visual evidence intervals.
The paper states that data, annotations, and evaluation framework are publicly released (pages 3 and 11); availability was not independently checked.
profiles.focus: Audio-visual answering and temporal evidence localization on 1,027 human-annotated questions over 392 recorded videos collected from open platforms. Models receive preprocessed video frames and corresponding audio and return an answer plus separate audio and visual timestamp intervals (pages 5, 8, 16, and 19).
profiles.limits: This is analysis of prerecorded media, without simulator actions, device control, executed research experiments, or new physical measurements. Temporal overlap establishes localization agreement, not semantic understanding or causal use of evidence (page 32). Coverage scoring permits broad intervals. Video selection constrains duration and content, and human participants may pause and replay, unlike the model inference protocol (pages 6, 17, and 33).

training.reward: A training reward or online learning loop is not established. Evaluation uses human reference options and evidence intervals. Answer accuracy scores option correctness; Coverage Grounded Score multiplies correctness by the average audio and visual evidence hit rates; Bottleneck Grounded Score multiplies correctness by the smaller modality-specific temporal IoU (pages 5–6). Failed inference, parsing, or truncated output receives zero scores and remains in the denominator (page 32).
training.reset: Environment reset support is not established. Inputs are fixed recordings. Human pause and replay permission is documented on page 17, but does not establish an agent environment reset interface.
training.branching: Agent-controlled branching or state forking is not established. Modality ablations and repeated evaluations change evaluation conditions rather than branch an interactive environment.

profiles.name: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning

openness: Finite option sets and probability predictions on fixed released evaluation items.
Seven core generators support fresh samples with configurable seeds (page 4).
Core data are stated to use CC BY 4.0 and code Apache-2.0; reference items retain source-specific terms, and access conditions restrict items to evaluation use (pages 7–8).
profiles.focus: Decision correctness, controlled contrast-group correctness, probability ordering, calibration, and selective coverage. The core contains 7,800 generated written cases in 13 families with computed answers checked by independent solvers. The reference track contains 32,233 fixed items from 35 public sets with human, programmatic, or mixed labels (pages 4–8).
profiles.limits: Models receive a written state, question, and finite options and return probabilities.
